At a glance, the game is fun. The gameplay gently challenges you so you'll observe, learn, and adapt. Guided by your newfound knowledge, you navigate the uncertain waters of RNG-reliant gameplay, sailing swiftly towards victory with style and flair—such is the story of any good roguelike. For one night of fun, I do recommend trying Merge Maestro if you'd like. In a world of $80 Mario, the $3 price tag is not obstructive. There's even a free demo! However... After my experiences playing, I was surprised to see this game is not in early access. The developer here has some very clear strengths and weaknesses. Whereas games like Balatro feel well-rounded between presentation and gameplay, Merge Maestro feels more clumsily-hewn, as if made with less wisdom and insight to guide it. I'll discuss the visuals, the audio, the gameplay, and then the surprisingly-spooky settings menu. So... the visuals. The main visual feature is the Emoji tokens/enemies. Super Auto Pets did it too. Emojis work for game dev if you don't really know how to make the art yourself. I would still argue that the emojis are used pretty heavily as a crutch. However, I forgive this imbalance in visual design compared to the gameplay, because the UI design is nice, and the game is generally pleasant to look at... out of the box, at least. We'll get back to that. The music... you know what you're getting into the moment you hear it. This game loops the same three (or so) royalty-free tunes back-to-back. Well, either they're royalty-free, or whoever composed and produced this soundtrack must view Kevin MacLeod as a paragon of what music ought to be. The music is fine at first, but eventually I found it to be so grating that I had to turn it off and put on my own music—which mentally took me out of the gameplay experience somewhat. If I were rating this game out of ten, the music would be worth docking two points. The SFX, by comparison, are quite pleasant and fitting! Okay. The gameplay was good at the start, but I developed problems with it. First off, I suddenly seemed to stop enjoying the gameplay the moment I unlocked the sports pack. You get five packs in your game at random, and you only get to guarantee one of them for each match. I have seven packs currently unlocked, so with my one pick guaranteed, the sports pack will be added 4/6 times. The sports pack introduces the mechanic of exhausting and un-exhausting certain tokens (exhausted means it can do nothing but sit there), as well "practicing" certain sports (i.e. introducing temporary improvements for specific token types in the sports pack—the improvements counting down in duration every turn). This pack does not fit gracefully among the previous six, and is far more rigorous to learn and adopt. It requires so many compatible tokens in your deck JUST to function AT ALL. It's like having a choir of five men, except one of them is going way too hard, and demands you accept him as the primary subject of your attention for the entire show, if you are to enjoy it. He is not the main singer, even if he fancies himself so. This would be acceptable for me if I found the sports pack fun, but I disliked it so much that I burnt out from playing before unlocking the final 3 packs. The sports pack clogs all my choices, and its presence throws off my flow. To cap things off: a Lovecraftian horror story about my fun Tornado build with heavy countdown reduction—or, how the façade of elegant design collapsed at its foundation. Note: forgive any misnamed tokens/perks; as of this review, there is no Merge Maestro wiki for me to refer to. So, the Tornado token (level 5) will sit on your board, counting down from 5 every turn. Upon counting 0, it attacks the first enemy 5 times for 1 damage each (by default). I had the Tornado+ token, which actually fires 10 attacks instead of 5. Cool. So I put a bunch of Tornadoes onto the board, and also use the Raincloud token (level 4) to reduce the countdown by 2 of every token on the board every time the Raincloud appears. I also got a perk (Storm+ or something) which, by virtue of not being a token, passively reduced the countdown of *all tokens* by 4 every turn for the rest of the game. On top of THAT, I got the Sun token (level 6) which, upon appearing, it reduces the MAX countdown of all tokens currently on the board by 2 (YEAH THAT'S INSANE). Do you see where this is going? Through "sound decision-making" I find myself with Tornadoes that fire off like crazy, doing 1 damage per hit. So like, every turn my tornadoes can pump out 50 or so hits. Imagine my face then, when I encounter the enemy that wears a life vest, reducing each hit's damage by 3. I now do no damage, which is definitely a skill issue! It seems I have hit a clear roadblock based on an unbalanced build. I guess I should, you know, try to rebalance my build by getting a fitting token from the end-of-wave token shop. You guys know how in Balatro, as your turn goes on, the scoring accelerates more and more until your turn finishes? It's like the heat is building up. Well, in Merge Maestro, there is no such mechanic. Every 0-damage attack from my tornadoes took the same amount of time. Therefore, now each turn included over a minute of sitting, staring, and waiting. I slogged through a few turns of this, listening to the grating royalty-free music, waiting to check the shop. I get to the shop. No remedy. I reroll a few times. No remedy. Gotta wait til the next shop then. "Oh, you know what?" I thought. "This game, much like Balatro, introduced a customizable CRT filter." Humor this tangent and ask yourself: when was the last time you saw an emoji on a CRT screen? Never? I'd say if you ever have, it was on the CRT screen you're reading this on right now. If that's you: nice hobby you've got there! Well anyways, the CRT shader actually looks terrible and unfitting on all settings regardless (sorry, not sorry). I thought "What if, much like with Balatro's (excellent) CRT shader, this game also appropriated Balatro's (excellent) game speed modifier setting?" Well, this game does have such a setting! In Balatro, I always turn it up to 4x. So, in this game, I attempted so—but I could only set it to 1x, 2x, 3x, 5x, and 10x. Not a problem, though—perhaps my Balatro comparisons were silly after all. I compromised, and tried 3x. As a result, the token placement animations moved way too fast, and the enemy bobbing animations looked like they're having a seizure. The turns still went too slowly, so I turned it up to 10x. It's clear that game speed should *only* affect "scoring" animations, not passive ones—lest we make this game into a violently-vibrating animal party, as I then experienced. It hurt to look at. The game speed setting serves very clumsily as a crutch—implemented without a clear understanding of, or vision for, its purpose. The turn duration issue NEEDS to be solved on a foundational level much like Balatro did, so the game does not necessitate this messy stopgap just to get you through your turns in a timely manner. To me, this specific issue felt emblematic of the whole game experience. The game is quite good at certain things, but in its shortcomings—from audio, to visuals, to game design—it over-relies on crutches to resolve those issues. Many subtle-yet-crucial issues go neglected—much to the detriment of the game as a whole. Some features are put in without too much thought about *why* they are good in other games—resulting in them not being very good in this game. Compounding on the more ill-conceived of this game's features, the game's clumsy stopgaps fail to stop underlying problems from creeping up and making the game feel less solid, less enjoyable, and less worthy of my time. ... but it's only $3! 🎉

Wish this could be a neutral review instead of a 'negative' one. I want to keep playing this so bad, but the amount of anti-synergy is too painful. When you get 3+ tokens from the same set that synergize, it's a very fun experience. As if getting multiple tokens from same set weren't hard enough (let alone upgraded tokens from the same set), many of the different sets take away from the viability of another. Fruit/consumables is a giant hassle to try to find board space for everything before it's automatically filled in by fruit - then you have to take a valuable action to free up a board space, while being lucky if the fruit has any synergy w/ whatever happens to be on the board (often it doesn't). Trying to go for sports & accidentally exhaust (temporarily disable) a higher value token? Well good luck finding something that lets it exit that state - and your run is ruined while you're at it. Trying to go for merge synergy but can't get any token in slot 3 to benefit from your powerful merge-buff effect from your slot 2? sorry, better luck next time. I did play today & a nice feature was added - whenever an effect would automatically change what was in any given slot, you now have the choice to disregard that where before it wasn't optional. Great improvement & I have hopes that this game could one day perfectly scratch the itch I have for combine-heavy roguelikes!

Simply put the most underrated roguelike deckbuilder on Steam. The game features a variety of depth and a plethora of mechanics but all are drip-fed to you so it never feels overwhelming. Difficulty is gradual and each one offers a fair challenge. Challenge runs offer interesting rules and restrictions and open up strategies not possible in the standard mode. The free demo offers a good 1-2 hours of content and the full game is well worth its $4 price tag.

Merge Maestro is a delightful game with a minimalist style and straightforward gameplay, lower difficulties can be light and casual whilst higher difficulties demanding. It punches above its weight with a level of polish, interlocking synergies, and gameplay options that far surpass what I expected from the simple and cutesy appearance of the game. As far as the gameplay goes I would emphasise this is a puzzle/arcade game more than a roguelike game. You get to draft tokens and form a custom build each game which keeps things fresh but it is a lot less RNG inclined than other roguelikes. Overall a sneakily good game and easily worth the low asking price simply for the underlying care and polish that has been put into it.

Solid simple premise which has a surprising amount of depth to it. Probably not the kind of thing that you're going to play for 500 hours, but has enough depth and variety that you could put considerably more time into it than I have. The main potential issue is that there is a lot of luck involved. While I think the game gives you enough tools that you probably could get consistent on the highest difficulty levels, the vast majority of people will never get there. Even having beaten all of the content the game offers, my win rate on the hardest modes probably wouldn't be over 15-20%. Some people may find this frustrating, though I personally didn't.

Firstly - Most of my issues stem from the highest difficulty. Up until (much like another reviewer had stated) the 10 hour mark, the game flows great. However, the game gets more difficult the more you unlock. The final difficulty isn't "necessary" to beat to have a fun experience, but it's nearly impossible to beat unless you get a good / cheese strategy going. The issue is that the final boss in the hardest difficulty is relentless. It's very, very hard to counter and do 200+ damage per turn - and in some cases, have to do 200+ damage 3 (even up to 5) times per turn - without having lucked out on your tokens. It's a great, super fun game. It's not too hard to get really into. The token pool expands greatly the more you play, which makes it harder to find what works well together in any given run. You also only get the selection of 1 out of 5 packs, which is fine in most cases. However, it becomes apparent there's some balance issues, and have 4 of the 5 with very few damaging tokens that can appear (especially at the lower 1-4 numbers). A lot of the early game tokens you want (do 3 damage - do 1 damage 3 times - create a level 1 token when using this level 2 token - create a level 1 token at the end of each wave - etc...) are only really in 2 or 3 packs, and they're not automatically guaranteed. Even if you get 1 or 2 of those, you still aren't guaranteed to ever even see these tokens. That makes the game extremely different each time you play it though, so it's a bit difficult to be really harsh with it. There's a lot of obvious "exploits" you can do that are quite fun to discover. I accidentally kept making my tokens in the queue go to a level 4 or 5 infinitely in one run. It actually made it WORSE for me, but it was hilarious. There's issues though, especially in certain tokens that are near impossible to find combinations with. Having something that creates consumables only after being destroyed is an example. They're very difficult to play around, as well as triggering their destroyed effect. The same goes for exhausted tokens. Having a level 7 token become exhausted because it accidentally got the last hit on the final enemy of a stage is infuriating, and in MOST cases, you cannot wake it back up. I highly recommend people who play this game to take it slower than I have. I play most games like this rather mindlessly and luck through winning a lot of the time. At higher difficulties, you need a legit strategy and idea on what to do. The game allows you to see what enemies you will be facing and that's something I knew about from the start, but never used it. I am going to come back to the game and play it slower, as I think that's the only true way to win consistently. I may sound like I complained a lot but it's frustrating due to how CLOSE it is to being a top game of mine. Even if the tokens are simple and goofy looking, they have a certain charm. The music isn't the greatest but it's serviceable. The variety of abilities is curious. I haven't seen all level 9 tokens still. There's tons of other combos I guarantee I've missed out on due to not realizing you could do them! It's a great game to tinker with. You can learn something new each time you play. Overall, I give it an easy recommend if you like the genre. There's far more positives than negatives. It's WELL worth the price, even if most people would only probably only want to play 10~ hours, or would prefer playing at lower difficulties.
